A batrachian or amphibian of the family ''Bufonidæ'' or some related family. {{smaller|Toads are generally distinguished among the salient tailless batrachians from the frogs, in that they are not aquatic (except when breeding), and lack the symmetry and agility of frogs; but the strong technical differences between the bufoniform and raniform amphibians are not always reflected in the various applications of these popular names. (Compare the common use of ''frog'' and ''toad'' in ''tree-frog'', ''tree-toad'', and in ''nurse-frog'' and ''obstetrical toad''.) Toads have a stout clumsy body more or less covered with warts, generally large parotoids (see cut under ''parotoid''), no teeth, the hind feet scarcely or not webbed, and the hind limbs not fitted for extensive leaping. They are perfectly harmless, notwithstanding many popular superstitions to the contrary. They feed mainly on insects, and some are quite useful in gardens. They are tenacious of life, like most reptiles, but there is no truth in the stories of their living in solid rock. There are numerous kinds of toads, found in nearly all parts of the world. They are mostly of the genus ''Bufo'', as well as of the family ''Bufonidæ'', though several other families include species to which the popular name applies. <noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|to|6360|toad-back}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Third son ''to'' the third Edward King of England.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 4. 84.}}}}

{{smaller block|An olde Cubbord. . . . A Carpett ''to'' the same of yelowe & tawnie satten embroderyd.
{{right|Quoted in ''H. Hall's'' Society in Elizabethan Age, App. I.}}}}

{{smaller block|Heels ''to'' his shoes so monstrously high that he had three or four times fallen down had he not been supported by his friend.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 48.}}}}

{{smaller block|In nine days the Maharajah Dhuleep Singh once shot at Elveden 2530 partridges ''to'' his own gun.
{{right|''Quarterly Rev.'', CXXVII. 386.}}}}

'''15.''' In a great variety of cases ''to'' supplies the place of the dative in other languages: it connects transitive verbs with their indirect or distant objects, and adjectives, nouns, and neuter or passive verbs with a following noun which limits their action.

{{smaller block|Better bowe than breke; obey ''to'' thi bettere.
{{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 65.}}}}

{{smaller block|Is it nothing ''to'' you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow.
{{right|Lam. i. 12.}}}}

{{smaller block|Drink ''to'' me only with thine eyes.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', The Forest, To Celia.}}}}

{{smaller block|This grand Conspiracy is discovered by Waltheoff ''to'' Lanfrank Archbishop of Canterbury.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 25.}}}}

{{smaller block|I am come ''to'' town, and ''to'' better hopes of seeing you.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Abs.'' Pray, sir, who is the lady?

''Sir A.'' What's that ''to'' you, sir?
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|After adjectives, it points to the person or thing with respect to which, or in whose interest, a quality is shown or perceived: as, a substance sweet ''to'' the taste; an event painful ''to'' the mind.}}

'''16.''' ''To'' is used as ordinary "sign" of the infinitive (like the corresponding ''zu'' in German, ''à'' and de in French, a and di in Italian, att in Swedish, etc.). {{smaller|In Anglo-Saxon, the verbal noun after ''tō'' took a special dative form — e. g., ''tō etanne'', 'to or for eating' — distinguishing it from the simple infinitive, as ''etan''; but this distinction of form has been long since lost, and the two constructions have also been confounded and mixed.}}

{{smaller block|And hopen that he be ''to'' comynge [i. e., to come] that shal hem releue.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xviii. 313.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thanne longen folk ''to'' gon on pilgrimages.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 12.}}}}

{{smaller block|A sower went forth ''to'' sow.
{{right|Mat. xiii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Ay, but ''to'' die, and go we know not where;
''To'' lie in cold obstruction and ''to'' rot;
This sensible warm motion ''to'' become
A kneaded clod.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1. 118.}}}}

{{smaller block|I am ''to'' blame ''to'' be so much in rage.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|He [the Almighty] is sharply provoked every moment, yet he punisheth ''to'' pardon, and forgives ''to'' forgive again.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., iii. 26.}}}}

{{smaller block|Many would like ''to'' make it a penal offence ''to'' preach discontent to the people.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 167.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''a'') ''To'' is not used before the infinitive after the ordinary auxiliaries, as ''do'', ''will'', ''can'', ''may'', etc.; also not after various other verbs, as, ''see'', ''hear'', ''let'', etc.; while after a few it is sometimes omitted or sometimes retained against more common usage to the contrary. After a noun or an adjective ''to'' is always used.}}

{{smaller block|Being mechanical, you ought not [''to''] walk
Upon a labouring day without the sign
Of your profession.
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 1. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|We are ready ''to'' try our fortunes
To the last man.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 2. 43.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''b'') ''To'' was formerly used even after another preposition, especially ''for'', and is still so used dialectally and vulgarly: as, what are you going ''for to'' do? Rarely after other prepositions}}, as ''from''; but very commonly after ''about'', ''about to'' signifying immediate futurity: as, he is ''about to'' go.

{{smaller block|For not to have been dipt in Lethe lake
Could save the sonne of Thetis ''from to'' die.
{{right|''Spenser'', Ruins of Time, l. 429.}}}}

{{smaller block|What went ye out ''for to'' see? {{right|Mat. xi. 9.}}}}

(''c'') After ''be'' and ''have'', the infinitive with ''to'' denotes something future, especially with the implication of duty or necessity: as, it is still ''to'' do (or ''to'' be done); I have it ''to'' do (or have ''to'' do it).

{{smaller block|We are still ''to'' seek for something else. {{right|''Bentley''.}}}}

(''d'') Colloquially, an infinitive after ''to'', when it is a repetition of a preceding infinitive, is often omitted: as, I don't go because I don't wish ''to''.

{{smaller block|You carry your business cares and projects about, instead of leaving them in the City, . . . or seeming ''to''.
{{right|''Dickens'', Little Dorrit, xxxiii.}}}}

{{smaller block|One can persuade himself, if he is determined ''to'', that certain of Shakspere's sonnets are of a biographical character. {{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', The Century, XXII. 913.}}}}

{{smaller block|Jack Barrett went to Quetta
Because they told him ''to''.
{{right|''R. Kipling'', Story of Uriah.}}}}

17. In various obsolete, provincial, or colloquial uses: after; against; at; by; for; in; of; on; with; before; etc.

{{smaller block|And go honte hardliche ''to'' hares and ''to'' foxes,
''To'' bores and ''to'' bockes that breketh a-doune menne hegges.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), ix. 28.}}}}

{{smaller block|Heo that trespasseth ''to'' trouthe.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), iii. 274.}}}}

{{smaller block|''To'' thee only trespassed haue I.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 252.}}}}

{{smaller block|My lorde ''to'' mete is he.
{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child's Ballads, V. 62).}}}}

{{smaller block|I mind when there wasn't a master mariner ''to'' Plymouth that thought there was aught west of the Land's End.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, xxx.}}}}

{{smaller block|He talks to himself, and keeps mainly ''to'' himself.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|John Kartor recd iij. yerdes of brod clothe, russet, to make a longe gowne ''to'' Sir John Walkyngton.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 321.}}}}

{{smaller block|Kutte nouhte youre mete eke as it were Felde men,
That ''to'' theyre mete haue suche an appetyte.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|Alle kynne creatures that ''to'' Crist beleuith.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), xi. 239.}}}}

{{smaller block|Therinne caste the calx of gold and sette it ''to'' the strong sunne in somer tyme.
{{right|''Book of Quinte Essence'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|Dickie he took good notice ''to'' that.
{{right|''Dick o' the Cow'' (Child's Ballads, VI. 72).}}}}

{{smaller block|Your most princely answer was, smelling ''to'' the gold—''Non olet'', it smells not of the means that have gotten it.
{{right|''Scott'', Fortunes of Nigel, xxxi.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thei . . . don me faste Fridaies ''to'' bred and ''to'' water.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), vii. 155.}}}}

{{smaller block|To knele on his knes ''to'' the cold erth,
And grete all his goddes with a good chere.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 798.}}}}

{{smaller block|We may hafe a desyre and a guet ȝernynge for to be present ''to'' Hym.
{{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 34.}}}}

{{smaller block|There 's naething the matter ''to'' thee.
{{right|''Lang Johnny Moir'' (Child's Ballads, IV. 275).}}}}

{{smaller block|You shall have no currant-jelly ''to'' your rice.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', in Lady Holland, p. 511.}}}}

{{smaller block|Stay, Amarillis, stay!
You are too fleet; 'tis two hours yet ''to'' day.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|At twenty minutes ''to'' three, Her Majesty . . . entered the House.
{{right|''First Year of a Silken Reign'', p. 36.}}}} Till to†. See ''till''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To a hair.''' See ''hair''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To boot.''' See ''boot''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To one's face,''' in presence and defiance of one.
{{smaller block|Weep'st thou for him ''to my face?''
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 77.}}}}
'''To one's hand.''' See ''hand.''—'''To one's teeth.''' See ''tooth.''—'''To the echo, the full, the halves,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''To wit.''' See ''wit, v.''—'''To you,''' a phrase of salutation or courtesy, equivalent to ''my service'' or ''my respects to you,'' or to ''the same to you.'' [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|"I should wish you to find from themselves whether your opinions is correct." "Sir, ''to you,''" says Cobbs; "that shall be done directly."
{{right|''Dickens'', Holly Tree, ii.}}}}
'''Would to God, would to Heaven,''' and similar precative phrases, are modern adaptations, with ''to'' inserted to note the direction of the wish or aspiration (perhaps after such phrases as "I make my vow ''to'' God," "I vow ''to'' God," etc.), of the earlier Middle English phrase ''wolde God,'' where ''God'' is the subject, and ''wolde'' the optative (subjunctive) imperfect of ''will'' as a principal verb; literally, "(I wish that) God ''would will'' (that . . . )." The words ''wolde God'' (in three syllables) could easily slide into the more modern-seeming ''would to God,'' where ''to'' is grammatically inexplicable.

'''II.''' ''adv.'' 1. To a place in view; forward; on.
{{smaller block|''To,'' Achilles! ''to,'' Ajax! ''to!''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 1. 119.}}}}

2. To the thing to be done: denoting motion and application to a thing.
{{smaller block|I will stand ''to'' and feed,
Although my last.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 3. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|"These plain viands being on table, I thought you might be tempted." "Thank 'ee, Mrs. Sparsit," said the whelp. And gloomily fell ''to.''
{{right|''Dickens'', Hard Times, ii. 10.}}}}

3. To its place; together: denoting the joining or closing of something separated or open: as, shut the door ''to.''
{{smaller block|Christ is brought asleep, and laid in his grave; and the door sealed ''to.''
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc., 1850), p. 102.}}}}

{{smaller block|He that hath received his testimony hath set ''to'' his seal that God is true.
{{right|John iii. 33.}}}}

{{smaller block|Can honour set ''to'' a leg? {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., v. 1. 133.}}}}

4. In a certain direction: as, sloped ''to''.

{{smaller block|Found in the nest three young owls with their feathers turned wrong end ''to'', . . . looking the very personification of fierceness.
{{right|''Amer. Nat.'', XXIII. 19.}}}}

'''Go to.''' {{smaller|See ''go''.}}—'''To and again.''' {{smaller|See ''again''.}}—'''To and back†.''' {{smaller|See ''back''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''To and fro.''' {{smaller|See ''fro''.}}—'''To bring to, to come to, to fall to, to heave to, to lie to''', etc. {{smaller|See the verbs.}}

'''III.†''' ''conj.'' Till.

{{smaller block|Pursue ''to'' [var. ''till''] thow a name hast wonne.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 2316.}}}}

{{smaller block|The rede see is ryght nere at hande,
Ther bus vs bide ''to'' we be thrall [taken captive].
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 90.}}}}

{{smaller block|Theys knyghtis never stynte ne blane,
''To'' thay unto the ceté wanne.
{{right|''MS. Lincoln'' A. i. 17, f. 116. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''to<sup>2</sup>†.''' An old spelling of ''too''<sup>1</sup>, ''toe'', ''two''.

'''to<sup>3</sup>''' (tō), ''n.'' [Jap., < Chinese ''tow'', a peck (or bushel).] A Japanese grain and liquid measure containing 1097.52 cubic inches, or a little less than half an imperial bushel.

'''to-<sup>1</sup>.''' A prefix of Anglo-Saxon origin, being the preposition and adverb ''to''<sup>1</sup> so used: as in ''to-name.'' {{smaller|In ''to-day'', ''to-morrow'', ''to-month'', ''to-night'', ''to-year'', it is not properly a prefix, but the preposition coalesced with its noun. In ''to-ward'' it is the adverb as the principal element, with suffix ''-ward''.}}

'''to-'''<sup>2</sup>. [< ME. ''to-'', ''te-'', < AS. ''tō-'' = OS. ''ti-'' = OFries. ''to-'', ''te-'', ''ti-'' = MLG. LG. ''te-'' = OHG. ''zir-'', ''zar-'', ''zur-'', ''zi-'', ''za-'', ''ze-'', MHG. ''zer-'', ''zur-'', ''zu-'', G. ''zer-'' = Goth. ''twis-'', apart, = L. ''dis-'', apart, away (see ''dis-'', ''dia-''). Parallel with this prefix is a noun-prefix OHG. ''zur-'' = Icel. ''tor-'' = Goth. ''tuz-'' = Gr. δυσ- = Skt. ''dus-'', evil, heavy (see ''dys-''); ult. connected with ''two'', ''twi-''.] A prefix of Anglo-Saxon origin, meaning 'apart, away,' and denoting separation, negation, or intensity. {{smaller|It is common in Anglo-Saxon and Middle English, but is almost wholly obsolete in English. A relic of its use remains in the archaic ''all to'' used as a quasi-adverb in ''all to break'', ''all to split'', ''all to broken'', etc., where the adverb is really ''all'', and ''to'' is properly a prefix of the verb, ''tobreak'', ''tosplit'', etc., in early modern English separated from the verb (being in Middle English, like other prefixes, commonly written separate), and often written with ''all'' as one word, ''alto'', taken as an adverb qualifying the verb. (See ''all'', ''adv.'', 1.) Such verbs are properly written without a hyphen; examples are ''tobeat'', ''tobear'', ''tobite'', ''toblast'', ''toblow'', ''toburst'' (''tobrest''), ''tobruise'', ''todeal'', ''tofall''. This prefix is often confused, by readers and editors of Middle English texts, with the preposition ''to'', the sign of the infinitive.}}

'''toad''' (tōd), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tode''; also Sc. ''tade'', ''taid'', ''taed'', ''ted''; < ME. ''tode'', ''toode'', ''tades'', ''tadde'', < AS. ''tādige'', ''tādie'', toad; root unknown. The Dan. ''tudse'', Sw. ''tåssa'', toad, are prob. unrelated. Hence, in comp., ''tadpole'', q. v.] 1. A batrachian or amphibian of the family ''Bufonidæ'' or some related family. {{smaller|Toads are generally distinguished among the salient tailless batrachians from the frogs, in that they are not aquatic (except when breeding), and lack the symmetry and agility of frogs; but the strong technical differences between the bufoniform and raniform amphibians are not always reflected in the various applications of these popular names. (Compare the common use of ''frog'' and ''toad'' in ''tree-frog'', ''tree-toad'', and in ''nurse-frog'' and ''obstetrical toad''.) Toads have a stout clumsy body more or less covered with warts, generally large parotoids (see cut under ''parotoid''), no teeth, the hind feet scarcely or not webbed, and the hind limbs not fitted for extensive leaping. They are perfectly harmless, notwithstanding many popular superstitions to the contrary. They feed mainly on insects, and some are quite useful in gardens. They are tenacious of life, like most reptiles, but there is no truth in the stories of their living in solid rock. The fable of the jewel in the toad's head may have some basis of fact in the piece of glistening cartilage which represents an unossified basioccipital. There are numerous kinds of toads, found in nearly all parts of the world. They are mostly of the genus ''Bufo'', as well as of the family ''Bufonidæ'', though several other families include species to which the popular name applies. In Europe the common toad is ''B. vulgaris''; the rush-toad or natterjack is ''B. calamita.'' The commonest toad of America is ''B. lentiginosus,'' which sports in many color-variations. See phrases below, and cuts under ''tadpole, Brachycephalus, Hylaplesia,'' and ''agua-toad.''}}

[[File:century v08 p0164 c3f1.png|center|360px]]
{{c|Common American Toad (''Bufo lentiginosus'').}}

2. Figuratively, a person as an object of disgust or aversion: also used in deprecating or half-affectionate raillery. Compare ''toadling.''

{{smaller block|"Yes," responded Abbot, "if she were a nice, pretty child, one might compassionate her forlornness; but one really can not care for such a little ''toad'' as that."
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë,'' Jane Eyre, iii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Accoucheur toad.''' Same as ''obstetrical toad.''—'''Cell-backed toad,''' a toad which carries its eggs and tadpoles in holes in the back; specifically, the Surinam toad. See cuts under ''Pipa'' and ''Nototrema.''—'''Horned toad''' (or '''frog'''), the popular name of all the small lizards of western North America with a flattened rounded form, the head horned, the back warty, and the habits sluggish. They are neither toads nor frogs (batrachians), but lacertilians or lizards, of quite another class of animals, and of the family ''Iguanidæ.'' All belong to the genus ''Phrynosoma,'' of which there are 8 or 9 species. See ''Phrynosoma'' (with cut). Also called ''toad-lizard.''—'''Midwife toad.''' Same as ''obstetrical toad.''—'''Obstetrical toad,''' the nurse-frog, ''Alytes obstetricans.'' See cut under ''Alytes.''—'''Running toad.''' Same as ''natterjack.''—'''Spade-footed toad.''' See ''Scaphiopus,'' and cut under ''spade-foot.''—'''Surinam toad,''' ''Pipa americana,'' a large and ugly toad representing the family ''Pipidæ.'' See ''Pipa'' and ''Aglossa.''—'''Toad in a (the) hole,''' in ''cookery,'' a piece of beef baked in batter.—'''Tree toad.''' See ''tree-toad.''—'''Walking toad.''' Same as ''natterjack.''}}

'''toadback''' (tōd′bak), ''n.'' A variety of potato.

{{smaller block|The ''toadback'' is nearly akin to the large Irish [potato], the skin almost black, and rough like a russetting.
{{right|''Amer. Nat.,'' XXIV. 316.}}}}

'''toad-back''' (tōd′bak), ''a.'' In ''carp.,'' resembling the back of a toad in section: said of a rail.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
